stops.narrative: The catalogue distinguishes a manuscript probably copied in Herat from its later illustration, probably in Bukhara. The painting makes patterns and arrangements visible. Other records explain teaching, endowed property and water maintenance; a literary scene does not identify every worker or household’s access to these resources.

Keep the carpet’s uncertain individual production centre separate from Isfahan and New Julfa’s documented urban relationships. Coercion in 1604 and settlement in 1605 preceded particular later commercial and household records. A 1700 merchant letter and a 1747 family letter, later than the 1598–1722 case, expose coordination and separation; neither identifies this carpet’s weavers, buyer or shipment.

The case is dated 1789, after Karim Khan’s death. Its supplied views show painted outer surfaces, a mirror and fitted storage. The catalogue describes an inner-lid gathering absent from these views. Separately dated accounts of building, merchants and artisans in Shiraz do not locate this case’s workshop or establish universal prosperity.

conclusion: Explain one task with a particular source. Then identify whose labor, household or access remains unknown. Material objects, institutional accounts and letters answer different questions; a capital, patron or decorated scene does not stand for all city life.

evidence.prompt: What can the supplied Bukhara manuscript photograph and its catalogue establish?

options.text: The arrangement is visible; the catalogue distinguishes likely copying and painting stages, with qualified places and dates.
options.feedback: Looking and catalogue research supply different evidence. The literary scene does not become a record of every household or worker.

options.text: The reception shows exactly how every household lived and obtained water.
options.feedback: A selected literary scene cannot establish universal living conditions. Water supply and access require other records.
